p: My name is Kuzey Aydın. I'm eleven. I'm a Windborn.

A few months ago, a storm told me my name, and my grandmother told me the truth. Seven bronze Keys hold the hearts of the seven great winds. Whoever brings all seven to the Gate of Seven Winds, and wakes it with a drop of the Keeper's blood, will rule the weather of the whole world.

Mordecai Vane, the Gray Hand, has wanted that for forty years. He was once my grandmother's student. He wanted to be a Windborn more than anything, and the winds never spoke to him. So he made a hand of stone that grabs the winds instead of asking them.

He kidnapped my grandmother to make me find the Keys for him. And I did. With my cousin Ela, my best friend Bora and Uncle Tarık, I found all of them, across the whole world. Istanbul. Crete. Iceland. Egypt. Japan. Mexico.
Three of them live inside me. The North Wind, the Black Wind and the wind of the desert.

Mordecai has the other four. He took the Lodos on Crete, the Gündoğusu on Mount Fuji, and the Poyraz under the city of the gods in Mexico, every time by freezing someone I love until I gave it up. And he found the seventh, the Kıble, the south wind, hidden under the Gate itself.
But his children have left him. Vera, who helped us in secret for months. And Vex, who chose us after I caught him in a pit in the dark.
Now my grandmother is waiting beside the Gate, eighteen floors under the ground in Cappadocia. And Mordecai is waiting for me.
I made a promise to the Black Wind, in an ice cave in Iceland. When it's over, all the winds will be free.
It's time to keep it.
**Kuzey Aydın,** 11. A Windborn. Three winds inside him. Can fly, badly. Has a letter for his parents in his pocket.
**Ela Aydın,** 12. Kuzey's cousin. Keeper of the Clue Book. Thinks she knows the answer. Doesn't know the question yet.
**Bora Kaya,** 11. Kuzey's best friend. Beastspeaker. Also known as EL GRAN BORA. Has bright red shoes.
**Vera Vane,** 13. Mordecai's daughter. Wants to study whales.
**Vex Vane,** 13. Mordecai's son. His right hand is stone. Carries his mother's compass. It always points at Kuzey.
**Uncle Tarık.** Ela's dad. Archaeologist. Has been frozen twice. Still brave.
**Grandma Nermin.** The Keeper. Beside the Gate. Knitting a blue scarf.
**Mordecai Vane.** The Gray Hand. Four Keys. A cracked arm. Running out of time.
The kettle in Grandma's kitchen was on the stove. Cold.
We stood in her flat in Kadıköy, the six of us, and nobody said anything.

I had left it boiling. On the day we went to the airport, all those weeks ago, I had filled it and lit the gas very low, so it would keep singing while we were gone. Mrs. Aksoy from downstairs must have turned it off. Of course she had. You can't leave a kettle on for two months. But I had hoped, somehow, stupidly, that it would still be singing when we got back.
It wasn't.

Everything else was exactly like the morning she disappeared. The teacups on the table. Her apron on its hook. The newspaper, open to the crossword, with half the answers filled in her neat handwriting. *Seven across: A wind from the north (6). POYRAZ.* The nine compasses on the shelf, where Ela and Bora and I had put them back, in the right order.
The smell of her. Cinnamon and old books.
Only the window was different. Somebody had fixed the glass that the storm had cracked, on the day it all began.
Outside, the ferries crossed the Bosphorus, and the seagulls screamed, and the city of Istanbul went on with its day, as if nothing in the world was wrong.

Paşa the cat came out from under the sofa. He looked at us. At me, and Ela, and Bora, and Uncle Tarık. Then at Vera and Vex, who were standing in the doorway, not sure if they were allowed to come in.
He walked straight past me. Straight past all of us. And went to Vex.
He sniffed Vex's shoes. He sniffed his stone hand, hanging at his side. Then he rubbed his whole body against Vex's legs, around and around, purring like a motorbike.
Vex stared down at him.
"He never does that," said Ela. "Paşa hates everybody. He hates *me.*"
"He says," said Bora slowly, "that Vex smells like Grandma. Like her tea. He says Vex has been near her. Recently." Bora looked at Vex. "He wants to know if she's okay."
Vex knelt down, very slowly, on the kitchen floor. He put out his human hand, his left one, and Paşa pushed his head into it.
"She's okay," Vex said quietly, to the cat. "She's knitting. She talks about you. She worries about who's feeding you."
Paşa purred louder.
Ela put her hand on my shoulder.
"She'll be back here," she said. "Soon. We'll make sure."
I went to the stove. I filled the kettle. I lit the gas.
And I waited. Until it started to hum. And then to whistle. And steam poured out of the spout and filled the kitchen with a soft warm cloud.
"There," I said. "Now it's a kitchen again."
Behind me, I heard Vera laugh. A small, wet laugh.
Bora's mother fed us.

She had known we were coming. Bora had called her from the airport in Mexico. She had cooked for two days. When we walked into her flat, two floors down from Bora's grandmother's, the table was so full of food that you couldn't see the tablecloth.

Börek. Five kinds. With cheese, with spinach, with meat, with potato, and a sweet one with sugar on top. Stuffed peppers. Stuffed vine leaves. A huge pot of red lentil soup. Pilaf with chickpeas. Meatballs. Yogurt with garlic and cucumber. Three kinds of salad. Bread still warm from the bakery. And for dessert, baklava, and rice pudding with cinnamon, and a cake.
"Mom," said Bora. "There are only seven of us."
"You are growing boys," said Bora's mother, whose name is Ayşe, and who is almost as big as Bora and twice as loud. "And girls. And you have been eating foreign food for two months. Sit. Eat."
We sat. We ate.

Vex sat at the end of the table. He didn't know what to do. He had never been to a dinner like this. You could tell. He sat very straight, with his hands in his lap. His stone hand in a glove. He didn't take anything.
Bora's mother looked at him.
She looked at him for a long time. At his thin face. At the dark circles under his eyes. At the glove.

Then she got up, and went around the table, and stood next to him. And she took the biggest piece of cheese börek on the table and put it on his plate. And then a piece of spinach börek. And a meatball. And some pilaf. And some soup.
"Eat," she said.
Vex looked up at her.
"I'm not..." he started. "I'm not really... I'm the..."

"I know who you are," said Bora's mother. "Bora told me. On the phone. Everything." She put her big warm hand on his head, the way she does with Bora. "And you are a boy who has not been fed properly for a very long time. Eat."
Vex looked down at the plate.
He picked up the cheese börek with his human hand. And he took a bite.
He chewed.
And then, at the end of the table, in Bora's mother's flat in Kadıköy, in front of everyone, Vex Vane started to cry.
Not loudly. He didn't make a sound. Tears just ran down his face, and dropped onto his plate, and he kept eating, and kept crying, and didn't stop.
Nobody said anything. Nobody looked at him. Very carefully. Bora's mother went back to her seat and talked loudly about the price of tomatoes.
Bora leaned over to me.
"I told him," he whispered. "In Mexico. On the plane. I told him everyone cries."
The next morning, we went to the Grand Bazaar.
Rıza Usta's shop was exactly where it had been. At the end of the dead-end alley, behind the street of old clocks. The window full of compasses. The sign on the door that said OPEN, which was a liar.
He was sitting behind his counter, polishing a compass, the way he had been on the day we first met him.
When he saw me, he put down the compass. He stood up, very slowly. And then he looked past me, at the others. At Ela and Bora and Uncle Tarık. And at Vera and Vex.
At Vex's stone hand.
His old face went very still.
"Mordecai's children," he said quietly.
"They're with us," I said quickly. "They're on our side. Vera's been helping us since Galata Tower. And Vex..."

"I know," said Rıza Usta. "The wind told me. The wind tells me everything, these days. It's very chatty, since you went away." He looked at Vex for a long time. "You have your mother's eyes, young man. Elizabeth's. I met her, once. She bought a compass from me. For your father. For his birthday." He smiled sadly. "A very good compass. I wonder if he still has it."
Vex didn't say anything. But I saw his hand go to his pocket. To the little silver compass.
Rıza Usta took us into the back room, behind the curtain, with the carpet and the cushions and the brass lamp. He made us apple tea. And he told us about the Gate.

"Nobody living has seen it," he said. "Except your grandmother, now. And Mordecai. Every Keeper is told where it is, when they are young. And they are told never, ever to go there. Not unless the world is ending." He stirred his tea. "The old books say it was not built by people. It was there before people. The winds made it. Or the earth. Or something older. The first people of the Order found it, and built their city on top of it, to hide it. And hid the Keys across the world. So that no one could ever bring them all together."
"What happens when it opens?" asked Ela. "Really? Not just 'whoever opens it controls the weather.' What actually *happens?*"

Rıza Usta looked at her with respect. "A good question, little detective. A very good question. Nobody has ever asked me that before." He was quiet for a moment. "The truth is, nobody knows. The Gate has never been opened. Not once. In all of history. The old books say only this: *When the seven are together, the Gate will open, and whoever stands before it will decide what the winds become.*"
"Decide," said Ela slowly. "Not *control.* Decide."
§CLUE Whoever stands before the Gate will decide what the winds become. Decide. Not control.

"That is what the words say," said Rıza Usta. "Mordecai has always read them as *control.* He has always believed that whoever stands before the Gate will become the master of the winds. Forever." He shrugged. "Perhaps he is right. Perhaps he is wrong. Words are slippery things. Like winds."
He looked at me.

"Kuzey," he said. "When you stand before the Gate, the winds will be listening. All of them. Every wind in the world. Whatever you say, they will hear." He put his old hand on mine. "Choose your words carefully."
It was Sunday. My parents called.
I sat on Grandma's sofa, with Uncle Tarık's laptop on my knees, and Paşa curled up next to me, and the kettle singing in the kitchen. And I waited.
The call connected. The little metal room. The round window. Snow and ice.
But my parents weren't wearing their orange jackets. They were wearing normal clothes. And they were smiling. Huge smiles. Both of them.
"KUZEY!"
The screen froze. On both of them, smiling. For ten seconds.

"...COMING HOME!" my mom was shouting, when it came back. "We're coming home! Early! The ship is going back to Chile for repairs, and we're getting on a plane from there! Three weeks, Kuzey! We'll be home in three weeks! For New Year!"
I couldn't speak.
"Kuzey? Are you there? Did it freeze again?"
"I'm here," I said. My voice came out strange. "Three weeks?"
"Three weeks!" said my dad. "And guess what. I'm bringing the penguin."
"You are *not* bringing the penguin," said my mom.
"I'm bringing a *picture* of the penguin," said my dad. "A big one. For the wall."
I laughed. Then I was crying. Then I was laughing again. Paşa got up and walked away, offended.
"Kuzey?" said my mom. Her face had changed. She was looking at me very closely. Through the screen. Through all those thousands of kilometers. The way only a mom can. "Kuzey, what's wrong?"
I looked at her frozen-then-unfrozen face. My mom. At the bottom of the world.
I thought about the letter in my coat pocket. The one I'd written in Japan. *There are some things I didn't tell you.*
"Nothing's wrong," I said. "Everything's... Mom, when you come home, I have to tell you something. A lot of things. A whole story. A really long one."
My mom looked at me for a long moment.
"Is it a good story?" she said.
I thought about it. About the cistern and the carpets and the Minotaur and the trolls and the Sphinx and the typhoon and the pit.
"It's going to be," I said. "I think. I hope. Ask me in three weeks."
My mom smiled. A slow smile.
"Okay," she said. "Three weeks. And Kuzey?"
"Yes?"
"Is Mum with you? Can I talk to her?"
My throat closed up. I couldn't answer.
Behind me, Uncle Tarık leaned into the picture.
"Not today, sister," he said gently. "But she'll be here when you get home. I promise. She'll be here, and she'll make tea."
My mom looked at her brother for a long time. Something passed between them, something I didn't understand.
"Okay, Tarık," she said quietly. "I'll hold you to that."
The screen froze. On my mom, looking serious, with her hand on the glass.
Then the call ended.

chapters.t: Chapter Five: The Wind of Home
p: That night, I couldn't sleep.

I lay in my own bed, in my own room, in Grandma's flat, for the first time in two months. It felt strange. Too soft. Too quiet. No hotel noises. No snoring in the next bed. Bora was sleeping on the floor in the living room with Vex. Ela and Vera were in Grandma's room. Uncle Tarık was on the sofa, with Paşa on his chest.
I got up and went to the window. I opened it.
The North Wind came in. The wind of the Black Sea. The wind of my own city. My own name. *Kuzey.* North. It ruffled my hair, the way Grandma used to.
*Welcome home, Windborn,* it said.
Not the Yıldız. Not the one inside me. The real wind. The wind outside. The wind of Istanbul.
"Hello," I said. "I'm back."

*We have all been waiting,* said the wind. *Every wind in the world is listening now. Did you know? The winds of Athens. The winds of the glacier. The desert. The mountain. The city of the gods. All of them. Listening. Waiting.* It swirled around the room, rustling the curtains. *Tomorrow, you go to the Gate. Whoever stands before it decides what happens to us. Forever.*
"I know," I said. "I won't let him own you."
*We know,* said the wind. *That is why we chose you. Long ago. Before you were born.*
And then, very faint, from somewhere far away, I heard something else.
Four winds. Far to the south and east. Deep under the ground. In the middle of Turkey.
Screaming.
The Lodos. The Gündoğusu. The Poyraz. And one I had never heard before. A hot, dry, angry wind. Full of sand and sun. The Kıble. The south wind.
All four of them, screaming, in a stone hand.
I put my forehead against the cold glass of the window.
"Hold on," I whispered. "I'm coming. Tomorrow. Hold on."
*They can hear you,* said the wind of Istanbul. *They are holding on.*
I stood at the window for a long time, looking out at the dark Bosphorus, and the lights of the ferries, and the bridges glowing across the water.
Then I went to the hallway. To the wall of photographs. The hundreds of them, in frames of every size, old and new.
And I found the one I had walked past, on the morning we left for Greece. *I didn't look closely at that one. I wish I had.*
Grandma, young, in black and white, with a group of students, in front of a university. Everyone very serious.
And at the edge of the photo, a thin, serious young man, with dark hair, holding a notebook.
Both of his hands were normal.
He was looking at Grandma. Not at the camera. At Grandma. The way you look at someone you admire more than anyone in the world.
Behind me, I heard footsteps. It was Vera. She couldn't sleep either.
She looked at the photo over my shoulder.
"That's him," she said quietly. "That's my father. Before."
We looked at it together for a long time.
"He looks happy," said Vera.
"Yes," I said. "He does."

chapters.t: Chapter Six: The Road to the Middle of the World
p: Cappadocia is in the very middle of Turkey. From Istanbul, it's a long way. Ten hours on the bus.

We could have flown. But Vex said the Grays would be watching the airports. And Vera said her father would be watching her card. So we took the night bus, like ordinary people, from the big bus station in Istanbul, with hundreds of other passengers and their suitcases and their bags of food.

Turkish buses are wonderful. They have big soft seats and little TV screens and a man called the *muavin* who walks up and down the aisle all night with a trolley, serving tea and coffee and little cakes, and pouring lemon cologne into everyone's hands so they can freshen up. Bora asked for cologne six times. He smelled like a lemon tree by the time we got to Ankara.
Vex sat next to me. By the window.

He didn't say much. He hadn't said much since the börek. He just watched out of the window, at the dark countryside sliding past. Every so often, he took out his mother's compass and looked at it. The needle always pointed at me. Then he put it away again.
"Can I ask you something?" I said, somewhere in the middle of the night.
"Okay."
"What's he going to do? Tomorrow. When we get there. What's his plan?"
Vex thought about it for a long time.

"He'll freeze someone," he said finally. "That's what he always does. That's what works. He'll freeze someone you love, and you'll give him your Keys. Because you always do." He looked at me. "He's counting on it. He's counting on you being soft. Like your grandmother."
"And if I'm not?"

"You are, though," said Vex. He almost smiled. "That's the thing. You are. You jumped into a pit for me. You'll give up the Keys to save Bora. Or Ela. Or your uncle. Or my sister." He looked back out of the window. "Or even me, probably. That's what he's counting on."
I didn't say anything.

"So you have to have a better plan," said Vex. "Than him. You have to think of something he hasn't thought of." He turned the compass over in his stone fingers. "And he's thought of everything. He always has. For forty years."
"Not everything," I said.
Vex looked at me.
"He's never asked the wind for anything," I said slowly. "Not once. He doesn't know how. He's never even thought of it." I looked out at the dark. "That's the thing he hasn't thought of."
Outside the window, the sky was turning gray in the east. The land was changing. Flat and wide and empty. Brown hills. Snow on the tops. A huge sky, bigger than any sky I'd ever seen.

And the wind out there was old. Very, very old. Older than Athens. Older than Egypt. Dry and cold and patient, blowing across the plateau the way it had blown since before there were people. Since before there were mountains.
*Windborn,* it said. Very slowly. Like a stone speaking. *You have come to the middle of the world.*
Cappadocia looks like a place from another planet.
The bus left us in the village of Göreme just as the sun came up. And I stepped off the bus and stopped. In the middle of the road. With my mouth open.

All around us, in every direction, there were towers of rock. Tall and pointed, like witches' hats. Like giant mushrooms. Like ice cream cones turned upside down. Pink and cream and gold and white, rising out of the valleys in their hundreds, in their thousands. Some were as tall as houses. Some were as tall as apartment buildings. Some had little hats of darker rock balanced on top, like a cap on a head.

And people had carved them. Doors and windows, cut into the soft rock. Staircases. Balconies. Little pigeon holes, in rows, high up on the cliffs. Thousands of years ago, people had lived inside them. Some people still did.

"Fairy chimneys," said Uncle Tarık. His voice was hushed. "That's what people call them. Volcanoes made the soft rock, millions of years ago. Ash, falling and falling, layer on layer. And the wind and the rain carved it into these shapes. Slowly. Over millions of years."
"The wind carved them," I said, looking up.

*Yes,* whispered a dry, ancient voice in the air. A voice that sounded like sand. Like stone. *We carved them all. We have been carving this land since before the first human. Every tower. Every valley.* A pause. *And we carved the Gate.*

That night, we stayed in a hotel inside a cave. A real one. Carved into the side of a fairy chimney. Our rooms had walls of pink stone and little round windows and beds built into the rock. There were carpets on the floor and lamps in little holes in the walls. The ceiling was curved, like being inside an egg.
Bora said it was the best hotel he had ever been in. Then he found out breakfast was included, and said it was the best hotel *anyone* had ever been in. In history.
But nobody could really enjoy it.
Because tomorrow was the day.

At dinner, in the cave restaurant, everyone was very quiet. Even Bora. He only had two plates of food. Uncle Tarık kept taking his glasses off and putting them back on. Vera kept looking at Vex. Vex kept looking at his compass.
And Ela had the Clue Book open next to her plate, and she wasn't eating at all. She was reading. Every page. From the very beginning.

chapters.t: Chapter Eight: Meanwhile, at the Bottom of the World
p: *Grandma told Kuzey this later.*
That night, Mordecai Vane stood in front of the Gate of Seven Winds, and put the Keys in.
Grandma Nermin watched him from the doorway of her little room. She didn't say anything. She just watched.

The chamber at the bottom of Derinkuyu was enormous. Round, like the inside of a drum, with a ceiling so high that the light didn't reach it. And in the middle of the floor was a compass rose. Carved into the stone, twenty meters wide. A seven-pointed star. At the end of each point, there was a small round hole. Just the right size for a bronze needle.
Mordecai walked to the first hole. He opened his stone fist.
He took out the Lodos. Cold and gray and dull. He knelt, very slowly, with a crack of stone knees. And he put it in.
The hole lit up. Pale blue. A soft, warm, watery light. The light of the southwest wind. Of the Mediterranean. Of summer.
The Lodos stopped screaming.
Mordecai went to the next hole. The Gündoğusu. He put it in. The hole lit up red-gold, like sunrise. The Gündoğusu stopped screaming.
The next. The Poyraz. It lit up green. Green as the Black Sea in winter. It stopped screaming.
The last one. The Kıble. The south wind. The one he had found under the Gate, buried in the rock, the week before. He put it in. It lit up gold. Hot, fierce, desert gold.
It stopped screaming.
The chamber was silent.

For the first time in months, there was no screaming at all. Just four soft lights, glowing in four points of the compass rose. Blue and red-gold and green and gold. And three empty holes, dark, waiting.
Mordecai stood up.
He looked at his stone hand. It was empty now. For the first time in months.
And it was destroyed.

The cracks had spread all the way up his arm, past his elbow, past his shoulder, across his chest. Gray stone, cracked and dry and dead, like an old riverbed. Little pieces fell off it when he moved. He could barely lift it.
He looked at it for a long time.
"Four," he said. "Three more. Tomorrow."
"Mordecai," said Grandma, from the doorway.
He didn't turn around.
"You know what happens," she said quietly, "when the stone reaches your heart."
"Yes," said Mordecai.
"Then why?"
He was quiet for a long, long time. Standing in the middle of the compass rose, with the four lights glowing around him.

"Because I'm so close," he said. "Because after forty years, I'm so close. Because tomorrow, the winds will have to listen to me. All of them. Forever." His voice cracked. "Because I can't stop now, Nermin. If I stop now, it was all for nothing. Elizabeth. The children. All of it. For nothing."
Grandma didn't say anything.
She went back into her little room, and sat down, and picked up her knitting.
The scarf was finished. Blue, with little white flowers. She held it in her lap and looked at it for a long time.
Then she took one end of it, and found the very last stitch, and pulled.
And very carefully, very slowly, she began to unravel it.
Ela didn't sleep. Of course she didn't.

I found her in the courtyard of the cave hotel at midnight, sitting on a stone bench under the stars, with the Clue Book on her knees and a flashlight in her mouth. The fairy chimneys rose around us in the dark, black against the stars, like a forest of giants. It was very cold. Our breath made clouds.

She had gone through every page. Every clue. Every riddle. From the very first one, in Istanbul. *Seven winds, seven Keys, one Gate.* The Medusa head. The Tower of the Winds. The rune stone. The Sphinx. The gates of the foxes. The kite with seven tails.
"Look," she said, when I sat down next to her. She took the flashlight out of her mouth. She pointed to the very first page.
On it, in her small neat writing, she had copied Grandma's letter, from the room under the Serpent Column. Months ago.
And under it, in different colored pens, all the things she had added since.
*If somebody takes something from you, it's never, ever your fault. It's theirs.* (Vera's mother's rule.)
*Kuzey is not allowed to say sorry for saving Dad.*
And at the bottom, in fresh ink, from the plane over the Atlantic:
*The winds cannot be owned. Only borrowed.*

"Your grandmother told us the answer at the very start," said Ela. "In her letter. And then she wrote it on the map. And Uncle Tarık remembered her saying it. In Crete. And the Feathered Serpent said it, sort of. And Fūjin said it. *It cannot make a wind love it.*" She tapped the page. "Everyone keeps saying the same thing. Over and over. In different ways. Like a clue. Like the biggest clue of all."
"What does it mean?" I said.

"I don't know," said Ela, frustrated. "That's the problem. I don't know what question it's the answer to." She pushed up her glasses. "Rıza Usta said, *whoever stands before the Gate will decide what the winds become.* Decide. Not control. And Mordecai thinks it means control. He's spent forty years thinking it means control." She frowned. "But what if it doesn't? What if it means something else? What if the Gate isn't a key that makes you the master? What if it's... a question?"
"A question?"

"Like the Sphinx," said Ela. "The Sphinx asked a question, and everyone gave clever answers. Long ones. Beautiful ones. And they were all wrong. Because they were too busy being clever to listen." She looked at me. "And you got it right. Because you just said the simplest thing. The thing everyone else was too clever to say."
"The wind," I said.

"The wind," said Ela. "So maybe the Gate is the same. Maybe it's asking a question. *What should the winds become?* And Mordecai has a clever answer. A long, complicated answer. *They should obey me. Forever.*" She closed the Clue Book. "And maybe the right answer is something simple. Something so simple that nobody's ever thought of it."
I looked up at the stars. At the fairy chimneys. At the dark shapes of the hills.
I thought about the Black Wind, in the ice cave in Iceland. *Free? No one has ever offered that before.*
"I think I know," I said slowly.
Ela turned to look at me.
"I think I've always known," I said. "Since the ice cave. I just didn't know it was the answer."
"What is it?"
I told her.
Ela was quiet for a long time. Then she opened the Clue Book again, to the very last page. And she wrote one word at the top.
*THE ANSWER.*
And under it, she didn't write anything at all. She just left it blank.
"I'll fill it in," she said, "when you've said it. At the Gate. So it's true."
"Derinkuyu has guards," said Vex.

It was five o'clock in the morning. We were sitting in a circle on the floor of my room in the cave hotel, with the leather map spread out in the middle, and a map of Derinkuyu that Uncle Tarık had printed out at the hotel reception. It was still dark outside.

"Grays at every entrance," said Vex. "Hundreds of them. Father's been bringing them through the fog for weeks. They're everywhere. On every floor. In every tunnel. You'll never get through the main entrance. Never."
"Then how?" said Ela.
Vex put his finger on the map. Not on the town. On a field. About three kilometers outside the town. Far away from everything.

"There's an air shaft," he said. "An old one. The oldest. It goes straight down. Eighteen floors. All the way to the bottom. The ancient people used it to bring fresh air into the city. So people could breathe, all the way down." He tapped the map. "The top of it is in the middle of this field. Covered by an old grate. Hidden in some bushes. Father doesn't know about it."
"How do *you* know about it?" said Ela.
Vex looked at his hands.

"Because I found it," he said quietly. "Two weeks ago. When I was bringing your grandmother her food. I was... I was looking for a way out. For me. In case..." He stopped. "In case I needed to run. I followed the air. From the bottom. All the way up. It took me three hours to climb."
Nobody said anything.
"The Grays don't guard it," said Vex. "Because Father doesn't know it's there. But there's a problem."
"What problem?" said Bora.

"It's in the middle of a big open field," said Vex. "Flat. No trees. No cover. And the Grays patrol the whole area. On the ground. In cars. You can see someone walking across that field from three kilometers away." He looked at me. "You can only get to it without being seen from the sky."
"From the sky," said Bora. He looked at me. Then he looked out of the little round window, where the sky was just starting to turn gray.
And in the gray, rising slowly over the fairy chimneys, there was something round. And red. And glowing.
A hot air balloon.
Then another. Yellow. And another. Blue. And another, striped like a candy.
"Oh no," said Bora.
"Oh yes," I said.
At six in the morning, the sky over Cappadocia filled with balloons.

Hundreds of them. Red and yellow and blue and green and purple and striped and checked and spotted. Rising slowly out of the valleys into the pink dawn sky, over the fairy chimneys, their burners roaring like dragons, *WHOOSH,* and then silence, and then *WHOOSH* again. They floated up and up, silently, gently, all together, like a slow-motion firework. The rising sun lit them up from one side, so that they glowed like lanterns.
It is the most beautiful thing I have ever seen. Even more beautiful than flying over Mount Fuji. Even more beautiful than the northern lights.
We weren't there to look at them, though.
We were there to steal one.
Well. Borrow one.

We went down to the launch field just before dawn. A big flat field at the edge of the village, covered in frost, where dozens of balloons were lying on the ground like huge sleeping animals, being filled with hot air. Men were running around with ropes. Big fans were roaring. Burners were blasting flames into the open mouths of the balloons, and slowly, slowly, they were swelling up, rising off the ground, standing up, and pulling at their ropes.
"Which one?" said Uncle Tarık. "And how? We can't just *take* one. We don't know how to fly one."
"I know how to fly one," I said. "Sort of. I'm the wind."
"That," said Ela, "is not the same thing."
Then a voice behind us said, "Kuzey Aydın?"
We all spun around.

An old man was standing there. He was very old, with a brown wrinkled face, and a huge white moustache that curled up at the ends like the horns of a ram. He was wearing a thick jacket and a woolly hat. And he was smiling.
"You're Nermin's boy," he said. "Aren't you? I knew you'd come. I've been waiting forty years."
Everyone in the Order, it seemed, had been waiting forty years.

His name was Hasan Amca. He had been a balloon pilot in Cappadocia for fifty years. And forty years ago, a woman with short silver hair and very sharp eyes had come to his field at dawn, and asked him to take her up in his balloon. And while they were floating over the fairy chimneys, she had told him that one day, a boy would come who could talk to the wind. And that the boy would need a balloon.

"I thought she was a bit strange," said Hasan Amca. "But I liked her very much. She made me promise. So I promised." He turned and pointed at a balloon, standing up at the edge of the field, almost full. A big red one. The reddest one there. "That one is mine. Get in."
Uncle Tarık looked at the balloon. Then at Hasan Amca.
"Can I pay you?" he said weakly. "I don't have any airline miles left. Or any money. But I could..."
"Pay me?" Hasan Amca laughed. A big laugh, that made his moustache shake. "Nermin already paid me. Forty years ago. She cured my mother's cough with a cup of tea." He pointed at the basket. "Get in."
We got in.

The basket was made of wicker, and it creaked. It was big enough for about ten people, with the burner in the middle, on a metal frame, roaring. Bora got in last. He had his eyes shut. He held onto the edge of the basket so tightly that his knuckles were white.
"I'm fine," he said. "I'm fine. I'm fine. I'm fine."
Hasan Amca pulled a lever. The burner roared. *WHOOSH.* A huge flame shot up into the red balloon above us. Heat blasted down on our heads.
And we lifted off the ground.

chapters.t: Chapter Twelve: The Field of Frost
p: It was so quiet.

That's what I remember most. When the burner was off, there was no sound at all. No engine. No wind, even, because we were moving with the wind, at exactly the same speed. Just silence. And the creak of the basket. And far below, very faint, a dog barking.

We floated up over the fairy chimneys, into the pink sky, among the other balloons. Hundreds of them, all around us, above and below, some so close that we could wave to the people in them. A little girl in a yellow balloon waved at Bora. Bora had his eyes shut. Vera waved back for him.

Below us, the land spread out like a map. The valleys of fairy chimneys, pink and gold in the sunrise. The little villages, with their houses carved into the rock. The fields, white with frost. The mountains on the horizon, covered in snow. And the great volcano, Erciyes, far away, huge and white, like a king on a throne.
Hasan Amca didn't ask any questions. He just stood by the burner, with his hand on the lever, and looked at me. And he winked.
"Go on, then," he said. "Talk to it."
I closed my eyes.
The wind of Cappadocia was the oldest wind I had ever met. Dry and cold and slow, like stone. Like the wind had been carving these rocks for so long that it had become a little bit like rock itself.
"Please," I said to it. "We need to go to a field. Three kilometers that way. Where there's an old air shaft. In the bushes. Please. Very quietly. Without anyone seeing."
The ancient wind thought about it for a long time.
*Nermin's boy,* it said at last. Slowly. Like a stone speaking. *She rode in this basket. Forty years ago. She asked us nicely too.* A pause. *We will take you.*
The balloon turned.

Very slowly. Away from the others. Out of the crowd of balloons. Across the valleys. Toward the north. Toward a big, flat, empty field, white with frost, with a line of bare bushes in the middle of it.
And then I saw them.
Black cars. On the road at the edge of the field. Three of them. And gray figures, standing beside them. Looking up.
And fog.
Rising from the field. Not normal fog. Gray, cold fog, thick and heavy, pouring out of the ground and rolling across the frost toward us. Rising up into the air. Rising toward the balloon. Fast.
"They've seen us," said Vex. His face was white. "They've seen us. He's making the fog. He's going to fill the whole sky with it. We won't be able to see anything. We'll crash."
The fog rose. It was already halfway up to us. Gray and cold and thick, like a wall. Swallowing the bushes. Swallowing the field. Coming up toward the basket.
"Kuzey!" said Ela. "Blow it away!"
"It's too big!" I said. "It's his fog! It's the fog road! It's coming from everywhere!"
The fog reached the bottom of the basket. Cold crept up through the wicker. Frost formed on the ropes.
And then I remembered.
I reached into my coat pocket. And I took out a small white cloth bag. No bigger than my hand. Tied with a red cord. It wriggled in my fingers like a hamster.
*A wind bag. It holds one breath of the east wind. The fastest wind in the world. When you need it, open it. Only once.*
I pulled the red cord.
The east wind came out of the bag like a dragon.

It was golden. Warm. Smelling of sunrise and cherry blossoms and the sea. And it was *fast.* So fast that I didn't even see it leave the bag. One second the bag was in my hand, and the next, there was a roar, and the whole sky was moving.
It hit the fog.

It didn't push it. It didn't blow it. It *burned* it. Like sunlight burning off morning mist. The gray fog turned gold, and then white, and then it was gone, in a great rushing whoosh, swept away across the field and over the hills and out of the sky, in about two seconds.

The black cars on the road were rocked so hard that one of them tipped over onto its side. The Grays standing beside them were blown flat on their backs in the frost, all of them, at the same time, perfectly in step, the way they did everything.
And the balloon shot forward.

Not up. Forward. Across the field. Fast. So fast that Uncle Tarık sat down in the bottom of the basket and Bora opened his eyes and screamed. Hasan Amca was laughing, holding onto his hat. The ground rushed past below us. The line of bushes rushed toward us.
And then the east wind was gone.
Used up. One breath. Finished.
And the balloon dropped. Very gently. Like a leaf. Right down into the middle of the field. Right next to the line of bare bushes.
And there, half hidden in the bushes, covered in dead leaves, there was a round stone hole in the ground. With an old rusty iron grate over the top.
The air shaft.
The basket bumped onto the frozen ground. *Thump.* We all fell over in a heap.
For a moment, nobody moved.
Then Bora said, from the bottom of the pile, "Can I open my eyes now?"
"Yes," said Ela.
He opened them. He looked up at the sky. At the red balloon above us, sagging slowly, empty. At the frost. At the bushes. At the rusty grate.
"Oh," he said. "We're down."
"We're down," I said.
"I'm never going in a balloon again," said Bora. "Never. Not even for börek."

Hasan Amca climbed out of the basket and looked at the field. At the black cars on the road, far away, one of them on its side. At the Grays, getting up out of the frost, slowly, and starting to walk toward us. Still a long way off. But coming.
He looked at me.
"Go," he said. "Quickly. I'll keep them busy."
"How?" said Uncle Tarık.
Hasan Amca smiled under his huge moustache. He pulled the lever on the burner. A huge flame roared up into the sagging red balloon. It started to swell again. To rise.

"I've been flying balloons for fifty years," he said. "I know a few tricks. And these gray men..." He looked at them, walking across the field toward us. "They don't look like they've ever been in a balloon. I think they'll find it very confusing."
He waved at us.
"Tell Nermin," he said, "that her tea still works. My mother is ninety-eight now."

The balloon rose up into the air, with Hasan Amca in the basket, and floated slowly across the field. Straight toward the Grays. Very low. So low that the basket was just above their heads. And as it went over them, Hasan Amca leaned out, and dropped something.
It was a rope. A long one. With a loop at the end.

It landed right around one of the Grays. Right around his middle. And the balloon kept rising. And the Gray, very confused, rose with it. Up off the ground. Dangling from the rope. Kicking his legs. Floating away over the field.
The other Grays stopped. They looked up at their friend, floating away in the sky.
They started to run after the balloon.
"*Go!*" shouted Hasan Amca, from the sky, laughing.
We went.
Bora and Uncle Tarık pulled the rusty grate off the air shaft. It came away with a long, horrible screech, and a shower of rust and dead leaves.
Underneath, the shaft went straight down into darkness.

It was round, and narrow, about as wide as a well. Carved out of the soft pink rock. Its walls were smooth, worn by thousands of years of air going up and down. We shone our flashlights down it. The light went down, and down, and down, and disappeared into black. There was no bottom. Not one that we could see.
And from very far below, a cold wind blew up out of it. A gray wind. A wind that smelled like frost. Like metal. Like a fridge.
He was down there.
There was a rope ladder. Old. Very old. Tied to an iron ring set into the stone at the top of the shaft. It hung down into the dark, swaying gently in the cold air.
"I put it there," said Vex. "Two weeks ago. When I climbed up. I found it in one of the storerooms on the third floor." He looked at it. "It held me. I think it'll hold everyone. One at a time."
"One at a time," repeated Uncle Tarık, looking at Bora.
"I'll go last," said Bora. "Then if I break it, everyone else is already down."
"Bora," said Ela.
"It's logic," said Bora. "You'd say the same thing."
Ela opened her mouth. Then she closed it. "Yes," she said. "I would."
I went first.

I could have flown. Floated down the shaft. But it was narrow, and dark, and I didn't know how far it went, and I didn't trust myself to fly in such a small space. So I took the rope ladder. And I started to climb down.
It was a very long way.

The light from the top got smaller and smaller. A circle. A coin. A dot. Then nothing. Only the light from the flashlight in my mouth, shining on the pink stone wall in front of my face. And the cold wind blowing up from below. And the creak of the rope.
Every so often, there was an opening in the wall of the shaft. A hole, leading off sideways into the dark. Another floor of the underground city. I counted them. One. Two. Three. Four.
Above me, I could hear Ela climbing down. Then Vera. Then Vex. Then Uncle Tarık, saying something in Latin on every rung.
And then, from very far above, Bora.
The rope creaked a lot when Bora got on it. It groaned. It stretched.
Eleven. Twelve. Thirteen.
And then, somewhere between floor fourteen and floor fifteen, I heard a sound.
A small sound. Very quiet.
*Snap.*
One of the strands of the rope ladder, just above me, had broken.
I looked up.

In the light of my flashlight, I could see it. About a meter above my head. One of the two long ropes that made the sides of the ladder had snapped. Just one strand of it, so far. The rope was old and dry and rotten, and it was unraveling, slowly, one thread at a time, like a sweater coming apart.
And above it, four people. Ela. Vera. Vex. Uncle Tarık. And above them, somewhere in the dark, Bora. All of them hanging on the same old rope.
*Snap.* Another strand.
"Everyone stop!" I shouted. "Don't move! The rope's breaking!"
Everyone stopped. In the dark above me, I heard Ela gasp.
"Where?" called Vex.
"Just above me! Between me and Ela!"
*Snap.*
The rope lurched. Everyone above me lurched with it. Uncle Tarık stopped saying Latin and started saying something much ruder. Bora, far above, said, "I'm fine. I'm fine. I'm *not fine.*"
I hung there, with one hand on the ladder and the flashlight in my mouth, and I thought very, very fast.
I could fly. I could catch one person, maybe. Two, if I was lucky. Like Vex in the pit. But not five. Not all at once. Not in a narrow shaft in the dark.
*Snap.*
And then I remembered.
I reached into my coat pocket. And I took out a wooden spool, with very old string wound around it. Gray and thin. It didn't look like much.
*The string from Nermin's kite. Very strong. Stronger than it looks. She made it herself, from the hair of a horse from the Black Sea. Use it when you need to hold on to something.*
I let go of the ladder.
I didn't fall. I asked the wind to hold me, and it did. The three winds inside me, holding me in the dark shaft like a hand. And I floated up, past the broken place, until I was level with it.
The rope was hanging by three threads. Three. I could see them, stretching. Thinner and thinner.

I unwound the kite string. My hands were shaking so much that I nearly dropped it. I wrapped it around the rope. Above the break. Below the break. Around and around and around. Tight. As tight as I could. The way Uncle Tarık had untangled his kite string on the bank of the Kamo River. Knot by knot. Very carefully.
I tied it off. Three knots. Grandma always taught me three knots.
*Snap.*
The last three threads of the old rope broke.
And the ladder dropped. About a centimeter.
And stopped.
The kite string held.

It stretched. It hummed, like a guitar string. It creaked. But it held. A thin gray string of horse hair from the Black Sea, made by my grandmother's hands forty years ago, holding five people over eighty meters of darkness.
Nobody breathed.
"Is everyone okay?" I called.
"I'm okay," said Ela. Her voice was very small.
"Okay," said Vera.
"Okay," said Vex.
"I'm going to have a lot of gray hair after this," said Uncle Tarık. "But okay."
"EL GRAN BORA," said Bora, from very far above, "IS OKAY. BUT ALSO VERY UPSET."
I laughed. I couldn't help it. I hung there in the dark shaft, holding onto the wind, with the kite string humming next to my face, and I laughed until my stomach hurt.
"Come on," I said. "Slowly. One at a time. Past the string. I'll be here."
They came down. One at a time. Past the place where the kite string was holding everything together. I floated next to it the whole time, ready to catch anyone who fell. Nobody fell.
Bora came last. Very slowly. With his eyes shut. When he got to the kite string, he stopped, and opened one eye, and looked at it.
"Thank you, Don Tomás," he said to the string. "And thank you, Grandma Nermin. And thank you, horse."
Then he kept climbing down.

chapters.t: Chapter Sixteen: The City Beneath the City
p: The ladder ended at the seventeenth floor.

There was an opening in the side of the shaft. A tunnel, going off sideways into the rock. Vex climbed into it first, and helped the rest of us in, one by one. Below us, the shaft kept going down, into the dark. One more floor. The eighteenth. The bottom.

"The Gate's down there," whispered Vex. "But we can't go straight down. There's a Gray at the bottom of the shaft. There always is. We have to go round. Through the tunnels. And down the last staircase."

Derinkuyu is a city underground, carved out of the soft rock, thousands of years ago. Floor after floor of rooms and tunnels and stairs, going down into the earth, like an upside-down skyscraper. People lived here. Thousands of them. When there were wars, or raids, they came down here with their animals and their food and their children, and hid for months, and nobody could find them.

There were kitchens, with black soot still on the ceilings from cooking fires. There were wells, deep and round, with water at the bottom. There were stables, with stone troughs where animals had eaten. There were wine cellars, with stone vats. There were bedrooms, little rooms carved into the rock, with stone shelves for beds. There was even a school, a long room with a stone bench along each side, and a church, with a cross carved into the wall.

And everywhere, everywhere, there were tunnels. Narrow and low and twisting. Going left, right, up, down. Splitting into two, into three. Dead ends. Loops. Some of them so low that you had to crawl. Some so narrow that you had to turn sideways. Bora had to turn sideways a lot.
"It's like the labyrinth in Crete," whispered Ela. "But worse."

"It's built to confuse people," whispered Uncle Tarık. "So if enemies came down, they'd get lost. And there are big round stone doors, look." He pointed his flashlight at a huge round stone, like a giant coin, as tall as a man, standing in a slot in the wall next to a tunnel opening. "They could roll those across the tunnels, from the inside. And nobody could get in."
We crept through the tunnels. Vex in front. He knew the way. Or he thought he did.

We heard Grays. Twice. Footsteps, in step, in a tunnel nearby. Cold air rolling around a corner. We hid in a stable, crouching behind a stone trough, holding our breath, while they walked past. Their fog eyes glowed in the dark as they passed the opening. They didn't see us.
Then Vex stopped.
"This is wrong," he said.
We were in a small room. A dead end. Three tunnels led out of it. Left, right and down.

"I don't recognize this," said Vex. He was turning around, looking at the walls, at the tunnels. His face was pale. "I came up the shaft. I've never come this way. I thought it would be easy to find the stairs from here. But I don't..." He swallowed. "I don't know which way."
"Kuzey," said Ela. "Can you feel the air? Like in Crete?"
I closed my eyes. I tried.

But the air down here was strange. It came from everywhere. Up from the air shafts. Down from the floors above. Through a hundred tunnels at once. Cold air and warm air, all mixed together. And under it all, that gray, frosty wind, from the Gate. It was coming from every direction at the same time.
"I can't," I said. "It's too mixed up. It's coming from everywhere."
Somewhere in the tunnels behind us, we heard footsteps. In step. Getting closer.
"We're lost," whispered Bora.
And then he went very still.
He reached up, slowly, and took off his hat. The hat with Krummi's feather in it. And beside the feather, a single white hair. Long and silver-white.
*If you are ever lost, hold it up, and a fox will find you. Anywhere in the world.*
Bora held it up. In the dark. In the light of the flashlight. The white hair glowed, very faintly, silver.
"Please," he whispered. "We're lost. Please."
Nothing happened.
The footsteps got closer.
Then, in the tunnel to the left, two little lights appeared. Low down. Near the floor.
Eyes. Gold eyes. Glowing in the dark.

chapters.t: Chapter Seventeen: The Fox of the Underground
p: It wasn't Shiro.

It was a fox, though. A real one. A red fox, small and thin, with a pointed face and black legs and a big bushy tail with a white tip. An Anatolian fox. A wild one. It stood in the tunnel opening, with its ears up, looking at us. At Bora. At the white hair in his hand.
It made a sound. A little yip.
Bora's face broke into a huge smile.

"She says," he whispered, "that a cousin in Japan sent a message. Through all the foxes. Across the whole world. From fox to fox. She says the message said, *A big boy with a cheese smell will hold up my hair. Help him.*" Bora's voice wobbled. "She says she's been waiting down here for three days."
The fox yipped again, impatiently, and turned, and trotted away into the tunnel on the left.
We followed her.

She led us through the tunnels like she had lived there her whole life. Maybe she had. Left. Right. Down a little slope. Through a low arch. Around a corner. She never hesitated. She never got lost. Every few meters, she stopped and looked back at Bora, to make sure he was still following, with her gold eyes glowing in the flashlight.
Behind us, the footsteps faded. The Grays had taken a different tunnel.

We went down a staircase. Then another. The air got colder. Grayer. The frosty wind from the Gate got stronger. And under it, I could feel something else. A hum. Deep and low, like a huge engine. Coming up through the rock, through my feet, into my bones.
Then the fox stopped.

In front of us, there was one of the big round stone doors. Rolled across the tunnel, blocking it completely. A huge stone wheel, as tall as Uncle Tarık, carved out of the rock. And on the front of it, there was writing. Carved into the stone. Old letters.
The fox sat down in front of it, and looked at us, and yipped.
"She says she can't open it," said Bora. "She says nobody can open it. Except the people who know the answer."
Uncle Tarık held his flashlight up to the writing.
"It's Greek," he said. "Old Greek. Byzantine. From about a thousand years ago." He squinted. "It's a riddle."
Of course it was a riddle.
Uncle Tarık read it out, slowly, translating as he went.
*I follow you all day, but I am gone at night.*
*I am always with you in the sun, but never in the dark.*
*I am as tall as a tower in the morning, and as small as a mouse at noon.*
*I have no weight, no voice, no breath. You cannot catch me, and I cannot leave you.*
*What am I?*
§CLUE I follow you all day, but I am gone at night. I am always with you in the sun, but never in the dark. I am as tall as a tower in the morning, and as small as a mouse at noon. What am I?
"A shadow," said Ela and Vera at exactly the same time.
They looked at each other. And grinned.
"It's an easy one," said Vera. "We had it in a code once. In Cairo. Remember?"
"Your code," said Ela. "Number seventeen. I cracked it in four minutes."
"Six," said Vera.
"Four."
"Six. I timed it."
"The answer," said Uncle Tarık, quite loudly, "is a shadow. Thank you, girls." He looked at the stone door. "But how do we tell it? Do we just... say it?"
"I think," said Ela, "we have to make one."
She took the flashlight from her dad. She held it up, and shone it at the stone door. And she put her hand in front of it.
A shadow fell on the stone. The shadow of Ela's hand. Big and dark.
Nothing happened.
"Not a hand," said Vera slowly. "Maybe it has to be a special shadow. Something to do with the Order."
I looked at the door. At the writing. At the carved border around the edge of it, faint and worn. Little pointed shapes. Seven of them. In a circle.
"A compass rose," I said.

Ela understood immediately. She handed the flashlight to Vera. Then she held up both her hands, and spread her fingers, and twisted them, and crossed them, one over the other, very carefully, until the shadow on the door made a shape.
A star. With seven points. Lopsided, and wobbly, and a bit strange. But seven points.
The stone door rumbled.
It shook. Dust poured down from the ceiling. And slowly, with a deep grinding roar, the huge round stone rolled sideways along its slot, into the wall. And the tunnel beyond it was open.
Ela lowered her hands. She was shaking.
"How did you do that?" said Bora. "With your fingers?"
"Practice," said Ela. "I've been practicing shadow puppets since I was five. Dad taught me." She looked at Uncle Tarık. "Remember? In the power cuts?"
Uncle Tarık looked at her. And his eyes went wet behind his glasses.
"I remember," he said.
The fox yipped. Once. Then she turned and looked at Bora, for a long moment, with her gold eyes.

"She says this is as far as she goes," said Bora quietly. "She says the place beyond is not for foxes. She says it smells of storms." He knelt down. "Thank you," he said to the fox. "Thank you so much. Tell Shiro thank you too."
The fox pushed her nose against his hand. Then she turned and trotted away, back into the dark tunnels, her white-tipped tail disappearing around a corner.
We went through the door.
On the other side of the stone door, there was a staircase.

The last one. Going down. Steep and narrow, carved into the rock, worn into dips in the middle by thousands of years of feet. At the bottom of it, a light was glowing. Not the cold gray light of Mordecai. A warm light. Seven colors, shifting and turning, like a rainbow trapped in a cave.
And on the top step, there was something.
Something blue.
It was a thread. A strand of blue wool. Thick and soft. Lying on the step, and running down the staircase, step by step, into the light. Like a path. Like a trail.
I picked up the end of it.
It was soft and warm, as if someone had been holding it. And it smelled of cinnamon.
"It's wool," said Ela. "Knitting wool."
"Grandma knits," I said. My voice came out strange. "She knits scarves. She was knitting one. Vex said."

"A blue one," said Vex quietly. "With white flowers. Like the one you're wearing. She was making it in the tower. And then down here. She said it was for someone special." He looked at the thread. "She must have unraveled it."

"Like Ariadne," whispered Ela. "In Crete. The princess who gave Theseus a ball of string. So he could find his way through the labyrinth." She looked at me, and her eyes were shining. "She unraveled her scarf, Kuzey. To show you the way. So you wouldn't get lost."
I held the blue thread in my hand. And I followed it.
Down the stairs. One step at a time. Holding the wool. It ran down the middle of the steps, down and down, never breaking, a long blue line in the rainbow light. Seventeen steps. Eighteen. Nineteen.
And at the very bottom, on the last step, the end of the thread was tied in a little bow.
Around a glass of tea.
A little tulip-shaped glass. Full. Still steaming. Dark red. With two sugar cubes on the saucer.
I stood there and looked at it. My eyes were stinging.
"She knew," said Ela softly. "She knew exactly when you'd come. She made you tea."
I picked up the glass. It was warm in my hands. I drank it. All of it. With both sugars.
It was the best tea I have ever had in my whole life.
§CLUE A blue woolen thread, unraveled from a scarf, running down the last staircase. Follow it. (Like Ariadne's string in Crete.)

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty: The Gate of Seven Winds
p: The chamber at the bottom of Derinkuyu was enormous.

Round, like the inside of a drum. With a ceiling so high that the light didn't reach it, and it just went up into darkness. The walls were smooth pink stone, curving up and up. And they were covered in carvings. Hundreds of them. Faces. Faces with puffed-out cheeks, blowing. Winds. Every kind of wind, from every country in the world. Greek winds and Egyptian winds and Japanese winds and Aztec winds and Viking winds and Turkish winds. Carved by people from every land, over thousands of years. All blowing toward the middle of the room.
In the center of the floor was the compass rose.

It was carved into the stone, twenty meters wide. A seven-pointed star. Exactly like the one on Grandma's map. Exactly like the one on the Medusa head, on Galata Tower, on the kite, on Rıza Usta's window, on Kaptan Murat's compass. The star I had been following around the world.
At the end of each point, there was a small round hole.
Four of them were glowing.
Blue. The Lodos. Soft and warm and watery, like the Mediterranean in summer.
Red-gold. The Gündoğusu. The sunrise.
Green. The Poyraz. The Black Sea in winter.
Gold. A hot, fierce, desert gold. The Kıble. The south wind. The one I had never met.
Three holes were dark. Empty. Waiting. North. Northwest. Southeast.
My three.
I could feel them, inside me, when I looked at those holes. The Yıldız. The Karayel. The Keşişleme. They went very still. Very quiet. Like people walking into a church.
At the far end of the chamber was a door.

Seven sides. No handle. No hinges. Carved with seven winds, blowing from seven directions, their cheeks puffed out like the winds on the Tower of the Winds in Athens. It wasn't made of stone. It wasn't made of anything I recognized. It looked like stone, but it shimmered, like heat over a road. Like it wasn't completely there.
It hummed.
The whole room hummed. A deep, low sound that I felt in my teeth. In my chest. In my bones. Like the whole earth was holding its breath.
The Gate of Seven Winds.
And beside the Gate, in front of a little stone room, at a little table, with a teapot on it (of course), sat Grandma Nermin.
She was thinner.

Her hair was messier. Longer. It was silver all the way through now, not just mostly. There were dark shadows under her eyes. There was a blanket around her shoulders, and gray chains around her ankles, made of something cold that steamed slightly, like dry ice. Her hands were wrapped around a glass of tea.
But she was sitting up straight. Very straight. The way she always sat. Like a queen.
And when she saw me, her face broke into the biggest smile in the world.
"Kuzey," she said. "My Kuzey. You took your time."
I ran.

I didn't care about anything else. Not the Gate, not the Keys, not Mordecai, not the Grays. I ran across the chamber, across the compass rose, past the glowing lights, and I threw my arms around her, and she dropped her tea glass, and it smashed on the floor, and neither of us cared.
She held me.

She smelled like cinnamon and old books and tea. Her arms were thin, but they held on so tight. Tighter than anything. And for a second, I was six years old again, in her kitchen, with the kettle singing and the wind blowing at the window.

"You were very brave," she whispered into my hair. "Very, very brave. I heard it all, you know. Through the winds. Every single thing. The giant in the cistern. The carpets in the bazaar." She laughed, a wet, wobbly laugh. "The *carpets,* Kuzey. Rıza told the whole Order. Everyone was talking about it."
"I missed you," I said. My voice was muffled in her blanket. "I missed you so much."
"I know," she said. "I know, my love. I missed you too. Every day. Every single day."
She held me at arm's length and looked at me. At my face. At my hair, which hadn't been cut for two months. At the scarf around my neck.
Her blue scarf. With the little white flowers.
She touched it, very gently.
"You've been wearing it," she said.
"Every day," I said. "You said to. In the letter. And on the wind. In Istanbul. *Tell him to wear a scarf.*"
Grandma Nermin laughed. And then she cried. And then she laughed again. And then she hugged me again, even harder.

Behind me, I heard the others come into the chamber. Slowly. Ela, with the Clue Book against her chest. Bora, with his red shoes and his hat. Uncle Tarık, with his umbrella. And Vera and Vex, side by side, holding hands.
Grandma looked up at them over my shoulder.
At Ela. At Bora. At Uncle Tarık.
"Hello, my darlings," she said. "Hello, Tarık. You look terrible. Have you been eating?"
"Not really, Mum," said Uncle Tarık. His voice cracked.
Then Grandma looked at Vera and Vex. Standing together. Holding hands. Vex's stone hand in Vera's.
Her face went very soft.
"And you two," she said. "You came."
"We came," said Vera.
Grandma looked at Vex for a long time. At his stone hand. At his face.
"Well done, Vex," she said quietly. "Well done."
Vex didn't say anything. He couldn't. He just nodded, very fast, and looked at the floor.
"Touching," said a voice from the shadows. "Truly."
Mordecai Vane stepped into the light.
He looked like a ghost.

His face was gray. Not pale. Gray. His cheeks were hollow. His eyes were sunk deep into his face, with dark rings around them. His long gray coat hung off him, as if it belonged to a much bigger man. He was leaning on the wall of the chamber, as if he couldn't stand up on his own.
And his arm.

His whole right arm was stone now. From his fingertips to his shoulder. Gray and cracked and crumbling, like an old statue left out in the rain for a thousand years. The cracks ran across his chest, under his shirt. Up his neck. Toward his face. Little pieces of stone fell off him with every breath, and drifted to the floor like ash.
Vera made a sound. A small, terrible sound. Like she'd been hit.
Vex didn't make any sound at all. He just stared.
Mordecai looked at his children. Standing together. Holding hands.
Something moved on his face. Then it was gone.

"Three more," he said. To me. His voice was hoarse. Rough. Like a voice that had been screaming, or like a voice that had been listening to screaming for a very long time. "Three more Keys, Kuzey. Inside you. And then the Gate opens. And it's over."
"Why?" I said.
I stood up. I stood in front of Grandma. I didn't know what else to do. My legs were shaking. But I stood there.
"Why do you even want it?" I said. "What will you *do* with all the weather in the world? You're sick. You're... you're turning into stone. Your children left you. What's the point?"
Mordecai looked at me for a long time.

Then, slowly, he pushed himself off the wall. He walked into the middle of the chamber. Into the middle of the compass rose. Between the four glowing lights and the three dark holes. And he stood there, swaying slightly.
"I was nineteen," he said, "when your grandmother told me I would never be a Windborn."
Grandma, behind me, went very still.

"She was kind about it," said Mordecai. "She was always kind. She said I could still help the Order. Read the books. Keep the maps. Be useful." His voice shook. "*Useful.* I didn't want to be useful. I wanted the winds to talk to me. Just once. I wanted them to *choose* me. The way they chose you. The way they chose her. The way they chose a little boy who had never read a single book."
He looked at his stone arm.

"I went to Japan," he said. "Did you know that? To Mount Kurama. To the tengu. I asked Sōjōbō to teach me to fly. I tried for a month. Every day. I fell two hundred and eleven times. I counted. And the wind never carried me. Not once. Not one centimeter." He laughed. A terrible, cracked laugh. "And you learned in one morning."
Nobody said anything.
"Then I met Elizabeth," said Mordecai.
His voice changed. It went soft. For the first time since I had met him, on the stairs of Grandma's building, it went completely soft.

"She was from the Order too. A Keeper's daughter. From Cornwall. She could hear the wind. A little. Not like you. Just a little. Whispers." He closed his eyes. "She used to tell me what it said. On the beach. On Sundays. She'd close her eyes and listen, and then she'd tell me. *It says the tide is coming in. It says there's a seal by the rocks. It says it likes your kite.*" He opened his eyes. "And it was enough. It was enough, for a while. Hearing it through her. Like listening to music through a wall."
He looked at Vera. At Vex.

"And then she died," he said. "And the music stopped. And I couldn't hear it at all. Not even through a wall. Nothing. Silence. Forever." His stone hand clenched. "So I found the old book. And I made the hand. If the winds wouldn't talk to me, I would *make* them listen. All of them. Every wind in the world. They would have to. Forever. And I would never, ever have to sit in the silence again."
The cracks on his neck had spread while he was talking. I could see them, creeping up toward his jaw.
"And my children," said Mordecai, looking at Vera and Vex, "will never be told they are not good enough. Not by anyone. Not by any wind."
"We never wanted that," said Vera. Her voice was breaking. "We never wanted that, Dad. We just wanted *you.* We just wanted you to come to the beach again. And do the voices."
Mordecai flinched. As if she had slapped him.
For a long moment, he just stood there. Swaying. In the middle of the compass rose. With his stone arm hanging at his side.
Then his face went hard again. Frozen. Like a lake in winter.
"It's too late for that," he said.
And he raised his stone hand.
The cold came.

It came out of him like a wave. White and freezing and roaring. It burst across the chamber, across the floor, up the walls. Ice exploded out of the stone floor, everywhere at once. Thick and white and crackling. Wrapping around Ela. Around Bora. Around Uncle Tarık. Climbing up their legs. Holding them.
Not hurting them. Not yet. Just holding them. Frozen to the floor, up to their knees. Up to their waists.
Ela screamed. Uncle Tarık tried to swing his umbrella, and it froze in his hand. Bora tried to pull his legs free, and couldn't, and shouted something that wasn't words.
The ice went for Vera.
And Vex stepped in front of her.
He pulled off his glove. His gray glove, on his stone hand. And he held up his stone hand, his own stone hand, in front of his sister, the way his father did.
And the ice stopped.
It hit Vex's hand, and stopped. Like a wave hitting a wall. Frost spread across his stone fingers, white and feathery, but it didn't go any further. It didn't touch Vera.
Mordecai stared at his son.
"Get out of the way, Vex," he said.
"No," said Vex.

His hand was shaking. His whole arm was shaking. The ice was pushing against it. I could see the cracks in Vex's hand getting deeper, spreading, up his wrist. He was using the hand. The way his father had taught him. And it was hurting him. Making it worse.
But he didn't move.
"Get *out* of the *way!*"

"No," said Vex again. His teeth were gritted. Tears were running down his face. "You said it stops hurting. You said after a while you stop feeling it. You *lied.* It never stops hurting. Never. And you know it. You *know* it."
Mordecai's face went white.
He pushed harder. The ice roared. Vex's arm buckled. He fell to one knee. But he kept his hand up. In front of his sister.
"Dad," said Vera, from behind him. Very quietly. "Dad. Please. Look at him. *Look* at him."
And for one second, Mordecai looked.
At his son. Thirteen years old. On his knees on the cold stone floor. Crying. With his hand turning to stone. Holding off his father's ice, to protect his sister.
Exactly the way his father had taught him.
The ice stopped.
Mordecai lowered his hand. Slowly. He was shaking. His face was doing something terrible. Something I had never seen it do before.
But it didn't last.

He turned away from his children. And he turned his stone hand toward me. Toward Grandma. Toward the ice holding Ela and Bora and Uncle Tarık. And the ice started to climb again. Up. To their chests. To their shoulders.
"Your Keys, Kuzey," he said. And his voice was cracking, like his hand. "Last chance."
I stood in the middle of the compass rose.

The Gate hummed behind me. My three winds burned in my chest. The North and the Black and the Southeast. Cold and stormy and hot. Grandma's scarf was around my neck. Grandma's tea was warm in my stomach. Grandma's hand was on my shoulder.
Ela was frozen to her chest. She was looking at me. Bora was frozen to his chest. He was looking at me. Uncle Tarık, frozen to his shoulders, his lips turning blue. Looking at me.
And Vex, on his knees. And Vera, kneeling next to him, holding his stone hand.
All of them. Looking at me.
And suddenly, I understood what Ela had figured out at midnight, under the stars.
*The winds cannot be owned. Only borrowed.*
"You don't need to take my Keys," I said to Mordecai. "I'll give them to the Gate myself."
"Kuzey!" Ela shouted, through the ice. "No!"
But Grandma, behind me, squeezed my shoulder.
She was smiling. I could feel it. Without even looking. She knew.
Mordecai stared at me. Suspicious. Confused.
"Why?" he said.
"Because it's not yours," I said. "And it's not mine. It never was. It's theirs."
I breathed out.

The Yıldız came out of me first. The North Wind. My wind. The one that had lived inside me since the night under the Serpent Column, in Istanbul, a hundred years ago. It came out in a silver stream of frost, glittering, beautiful. And it flew across the chamber, and into its hole, at the north point of the compass rose.
The hole lit up. Silver. Bright as a star.
*Thank you, Windborn,* whispered the North Wind, as it left me. *Thank you for asking.*

Then the Karayel. The Black Wind. From the ice cave in Iceland. It came out as a little black storm cloud, crackling with tiny lightning. It spun into its place at the northwest point. And lit up purple. Dark and deep.
*Remember the promise,* it whispered. *Remember.*
"I remember," I said.

Then the Keşişleme. The desert wind. From under the paws of the Sphinx. It came out of me in a swirl of golden sand. And it didn't say anything at all. Which was the strangest thing. The Keşişleme always said something.
It flew into its place at the southeast point. And lit up orange. Like a desert at sunset.
And I was empty.
For the first time in months, there was no wind inside me at all. It felt strange. Quiet. Lonely. Like a house when everybody has gone out.
I stood there in the middle of the compass rose.
Seven lights. Seven colors. Silver and purple and orange and blue and red-gold and green and gold. The whole chamber blazed like the inside of a rainbow.
Mordecai stared at the seven lights. His face was wild. Hungry.
"The Keeper's blood," he whispered. "The Gate needs the Keeper's blood. Nermin..."
"I know," said Grandma.
She walked forward. Slowly. Past me. In her chains, which clinked on the stone. To the very center of the compass rose. To the place where all seven points met.
She took a pin from her hair. A long silver hairpin, that she had worn every day of my life.
And she pricked her finger. Just a tiny prick.
One drop of blood fell onto the center of the compass rose.
"Not for you, Mordecai," said Grandma Nermin, very gently. "For him. I'm giving it to him."
And the Gate of Seven Winds opened.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Five: The Sky Under the Ground
p: It didn't swing open, like a door.
It *dissolved.* Like mist in the morning sun. The shimmering stone went thin, and pale, and then clear, like glass. And then it wasn't there at all.
And behind it was nothing.
Just sky.

A huge, blue, endless sky. Deep underground. Eighteen floors under the earth, under Cappadocia, under the fairy chimneys and the balloons and the frozen fields. A sky. With clouds in it. White ones, drifting. And sunlight, somehow, coming from somewhere. And moving air.
And the sound.

The sound of every wind on Earth. All at once. Every breeze that had ever blown. Every storm. Every gale. Every gentle sigh of air in a summer garden. The Poyraz on the Bosphorus and the Lodos on the Mediterranean, the winds of the Tower in Athens, the winds of the glacier, the desert, the mountain, the city of the gods. The wind that flew carpets in the Grand Bazaar. The wind that held up Shu's sky. The wind that pushed Abu Hassan's felucca up the Nile. The wind that carried a kite above the Kamo River, and a red balloon over Cappadocia. The wind that sang at a hospital window on the coldest night of the year.
All of them. Speaking at once. Listening at once. Waiting.
It was so loud that it was almost silent. Like the sea. Like the inside of a shell.
I stood in front of it, with my mouth open.
Mordecai laughed.

It was a wild laugh. A desperate laugh. The laugh of a man who has waited forty years for one moment, and here it is. He stumbled forward, past me, his long gray coat flapping, toward the open Gate, toward the sky. And he raised his stone hand. His crumbling, cracking, dying stone hand. High above his head.
"WINDS OF THE WORLD!" he shouted.
His voice echoed around the chamber. Into the sky.
"I COMMAND YOU! I AM MORDECAI VANE, AND I HAVE BROUGHT THE SEVEN TOGETHER! I HAVE OPENED THE GATE! I COMMAND YOU! *OBEY ME!*"
The winds went silent.
Completely silent. Every wind in the world. All at once.
The sky beyond the Gate went still. The clouds stopped moving. The air stopped.
Mordecai stood there with his hand in the air. Waiting.
Nothing happened.
Nothing at all.

The winds didn't answer him. They didn't obey him. They didn't fight him. They didn't do anything. They just... waited. Silent. Still. As if he hadn't said anything at all. As if he wasn't even there.
As if he was outside. In the cold. Looking through the window.
Mordecai's hand began to shake.
"Obey me," he said. Quieter now. "Please. *Obey me.*"
Silence.
Then I stepped forward.

I didn't raise my hand. I didn't shout. I just spoke. The way I spoke to the wind in Grandma's kitchen, on the day it all began. The way I spoke to the pigeons on Bora's roof. The way I'd always spoken to it, since I was tiny, since before I knew I was speaking to anyone at all.
"Hello," I said.
The sky beyond the Gate rippled. Just a little.
"I'm Kuzey," I said. "You know me. I'm the one who asks."
I took a deep breath.
"Winds of the world," I said. "I don't want to command you. Nobody should. Not him. Not me. Not anyone. You're not anybody's. You never were."
The sky rippled again. More. The clouds began, very slowly, to move.

"I promised the Black Wind," I said. "In the ice. In Iceland. I promised I would set you free. All of you. When it was over." My voice shook. "So that's my answer. That's what I decide. Since I'm the one standing here. Since the Gate says I get to decide."
I looked out at the endless sky.
"Go," I said. "You're free. Be wild. Be gentle. Be storms and breezes and hurricanes and the little puff of air when someone blows out birthday candles. Be whatever you want."
I swallowed.
"Just please," I said, "be kind to the people who live under you. Please. That's all I'm asking. Be kind."
For one long moment, nothing happened.

The whole chamber held its breath. Ela, frozen to her shoulders. Bora. Uncle Tarık. Vex and Vera, on their knees. Grandma, standing in the middle of the compass rose with one drop of blood on the stone in front of her. Mordecai, with his stone hand still raised, shaking.
Nothing.
Then every wind in the world answered at once.
It was the most beautiful sound I have ever heard.

Like laughter. Like music. Like the sea, and a thousand birds, and children playing, and rain on a roof, and a kettle singing, all at the same time. It came pouring out of the sky beyond the Gate, into the chamber, in a great warm rushing roar. And it was *happy.* So happy. Every wind in the world, laughing and singing and shouting, all at once.
*FREE!*
The seven Keys flew up out of the compass rose.

All seven of them. At the same time. Out of their holes, into the air. Silver and purple and orange and blue and red-gold and green and gold. They spun around me once, in a circle, like a crown of light. Like a halo. I could feel each one as it passed me.
*Thank you,* said the North Wind.
*You kept your promise,* said the Black Wind.
*Ha!* said the Keşişleme. *HA! Friends! I told you! Friends!*
And then they burst.

Each Key burst into a stream of colored wind. Seven streams. Seven colors. They shot up through the ceiling of the chamber, straight up, through the rock, through eighteen floors of underground city, through the earth, and out into the sky above Cappadocia.

I heard later that the people in the balloons saw it. Seven streams of colored light, bursting out of the ground in the middle of a frozen field, and shooting up into the sky, past the balloons, so close that the balloons spun around and around, and everyone in them screamed and then laughed. Seven rainbows, going straight up. Higher and higher. Spreading out. Across the whole sky. Across the whole world.
And the four winds that had been trapped in Mordecai's stone hand, the Lodos, the Gündoğusu, the Poyraz and the Kıble, remembered.
They remembered who had asked.
And who had taken.
Mordecai's gray hand cracked.
It cracked from his fingertips to his shoulder, with a sound like breaking ice on a lake. A huge, terrible crack, that echoed around the whole chamber.
And it shattered.
Pieces of gray stone exploded off his arm. Off his chest. Off his neck. They fell to the floor like hail, and turned to dust, and the dust blew away in the wind.

All the ice in the chamber shattered at the same moment. It burst into a million glittering pieces, all at once, like a giant glass breaking. And melted. Instantly. Into puddles. Ela and Bora and Uncle Tarık fell forward onto their hands and knees, gasping, free.
The gray chains on Grandma's ankles turned to fog, and drifted away.
And Mordecai fell.
Not down. Forward. Toward the open Gate. Toward the sky.

The winds were pouring out of the Gate now, a huge rushing river of air, and pouring back in, in a great spinning circle, the whole sky turning around and around. And Mordecai was too weak to stand against it. He had nothing left. No stone hand. No strength. Nothing. The wind caught his long gray coat like a sail, and it pulled him. Across the stone floor. Toward the edge. Toward the place where the floor ended and the endless sky began.
He didn't fight it. He didn't even try. He just slid. His eyes were closed. His face was gray and empty. As if he didn't care anymore. As if he'd given up.
"DAD!" screamed Vera.
Vex moved.
He moved faster than I have ever seen anyone move. Faster than me, jumping into the pit in Mexico. He threw himself across the floor of the chamber, on his stomach, and he reached out with his hand.
His stone hand. The right one.
And he grabbed his father's hand.
His father's stone hand. The right one. What was left of it.
Stone on stone.
They held.
