Mordecai stopped sliding. Right at the edge of the floor. With his legs hanging out over the endless sky. The wind roaring around him. And his son, lying flat on the stone floor, holding on to him with both hands, with his face screwed up, his teeth gritted, crying.
"I've got you," said Vex. "I've got you. I've got you."
Mordecai opened his eyes.
He looked up at his son.
"Let go, Vex," he whispered. "Let go. It's all right. I deserve it."
"NO!" Vex screamed. "No! You don't get to do that! You don't get to just leave! Not like Mom! Not again! You don't get to leave us again!"
Vera was there. She was lying next to her brother. She grabbed her father's other hand. His human hand. And held on.
And then I was there. And Bora. And Ela. And Uncle Tarık. And Grandma. All of us, grabbing. Grabbing Vex. Grabbing Vera. Grabbing coats and arms and legs. A human chain. Holding on.
And we pulled.
Bora is the strongest person I know. He pulled harder than anyone. He pulled with his whole body, with his red shoes braced against the stone, shouting.
Slowly. Slowly. Centimeter by centimeter.
Mordecai came back over the edge.
And we all fell backwards in a huge heap in the middle of the compass rose. Arms and legs everywhere. Bora at the bottom. Me on top of Ela. Uncle Tarık's umbrella somewhere in Bora's ear.
And in the middle of the heap, Vex and Vera. Holding on to their father. Both of them. So tight.
And Mordecai Vane, lying on the stone floor, holding on to them.
Behind us, the Gate of Seven Winds closed.

It didn't slam. It just faded. The sky went pale, and then misty, and then it was stone again. Just stone. A seven-sided door, carved with winds, in the wall of a chamber at the bottom of an underground city.
Quiet. Empty. Done.
The seven holes in the compass rose were dark.
The Keys were gone. Forever.
The winds were free.
For a long time, nobody moved.

We lay there in a heap in the middle of the compass rose, breathing. Just breathing. In the quiet. The chamber was very quiet now. No hum. No screaming. No roaring sky. Just the drip of melting ice, and our breathing, and somewhere, very far above us, through eighteen floors of rock, the faint sound of a dog barking.
Then Mordecai sat up.
Slowly. Very slowly. Like an old man. Vex and Vera sat up with him. They didn't let go of him. Not for a second.
He held up his right arm.
The stone was gone.

All of it. Every bit. From his fingertips to his shoulder. Gone. Shattered and blown away as dust. And underneath it, there was an arm. A real arm. Thin and pale and shaking. With a hand at the end of it. A human hand. With skin and fingernails and lines on the palm. Like it had been sleeping under the stone for forty years, waiting.
He looked at it for a long time.
He turned it over. Palm up. Palm down. He moved the fingers. One at a time. Slowly.
Then Vex made a sound.
He was looking at his own hand. His right hand. The one he had used to hold his father.
It was skin.

Pink, real, warm skin. From his fingertips to his wrist. The gray was gone. The cracks were gone. Every bit of stone. Gone. His hand was just a hand. A thirteen-year-old boy's hand, with a scrape on the knuckle and dirt under the nails.
He stared at it. He opened and closed his fingers. He touched his own face with it.
"It doesn't hurt," he whispered. "It doesn't hurt. It doesn't hurt anymore."
*Only the one who put it there can take it away,* the Feathered Serpent had said. *Or the winds themselves, when they are free.*
Vera grabbed her brother's hand. His real hand. And held it against her face. And cried.
Mordecai looked at his son's hand. And at his own.
Two real hands. Next to each other. A father's and a son's. The same shape. The same long fingers.
And then a breeze came down.

From above. From somewhere far, far above, down through the air shafts, down eighteen floors. A small one. A gentle, ordinary breeze. Not one of the seven. Not a great wind. Just the kind of breeze that comes through an open window on a summer afternoon. That rustles the curtains. That turns the pages of a book you've left on the table.
It came down into the chamber. It wandered across the floor, slowly, like a cat. It circled around us. Around the heap of people in the middle of the compass rose.
And it went to Mordecai.
It circled him once. Very slowly. It lifted a strand of his gray hair. And then it touched his face. Softly. Gently. On the cheek. The way a mother touches a child who is sleeping.
He gasped.
He went completely still. His eyes went wide. His mouth opened.
"It's..." he whispered. "It's..."
Tears were running down his face. Down his gray, hollow cheeks. He didn't wipe them away.
"It's talking to me," he whispered. "After forty years. It's talking. To *me.*"
"What's it saying?" asked Vera softly.
Mordecai closed his eyes. He listened. For a long, long time. His whole face listening.
"It's only saying hello," he said. His voice broke completely. "That's all. That's all it's saying. Just... hello."

Grandma Nermin got up. Slowly. Her knees cracked. She walked over to her old student. And she knelt down beside him, on the cold stone floor, in the middle of the compass rose. And she put her old, wrinkled hand on his shoulder.

"That's all it ever wanted to say, Mordecai," she said gently. "That's all it ever wanted to say to you. Hello. Every day. For forty years." She squeezed his shoulder. "You just had to stop shouting long enough to hear it."
Mordecai Vane bent forward, with his face in his two real hands.
And his children put their arms around him, one on each side.
And he cried like a little boy.
Ela came and stood next to me.

She was soaking wet from the melted ice. Her braids were dripping. Her glasses were fogged up. The Clue Book was pressed against her chest. She had kept it dry, somehow, the way she always did, even while she was frozen to the shoulders.
She put her hand in mine.
Bora came and stood on my other side. Sniffing loudly. Wiping his nose on his sleeve.
"I'm not crying," said Bora. "There's dust. From the hand."
"Sure," said Ela, wiping her own eyes.

Uncle Tarık stood behind us. He looked around the chamber. At the carvings of the winds on the walls, from every country in the world. At the compass rose on the floor, with its seven dark holes. At the closed Gate. At Grandma, kneeling beside Mordecai. At Vex and Vera.
"I am going to write," said Uncle Tarık, very quietly, "the best paper in the history of archaeology."
He paused.
"And nobody," he said, "will ever believe a single word of it."
Ela laughed. A wet, wobbly laugh.
Then she let go of my hand, and opened the Clue Book. To the very last page. The page where, last night, at midnight, under the stars, she had written two words at the top and left the rest blank.
*THE ANSWER.*
She took out her pencil. And she wrote, very carefully, in her small, neat handwriting:
*Free.*
She looked at it for a long time.
Then she closed the book, and hugged it to her chest.
"Case closed," she said.
We climbed up eighteen floors.

Slowly. It took a very long time. Mordecai couldn't walk properly. He was too weak. Vex held him up on one side and Bora held him up on the other. Grandma walked behind him, with her hand on his back. Uncle Tarık walked in front with the flashlight, the right way up.
Up the staircase from the Gate. Past the glass of tea, tied with blue wool. (I picked it up. I still have it. Ela says it's evidence.) Through the round stone door. Through the tunnels.
And in the tunnels, we met the Grays.
There were dozens of them. Standing in the passages. Sitting on the floor. Leaning against the walls. Wandering slowly through the underground rooms with confused faces.
And their eyes weren't gray anymore.
Brown. Blue. Green. Hazel. Normal eyes. Human eyes. Blinking in the light of Uncle Tarık's flashlight, as if they had just woken up from a very long sleep.

"Excuse me," said one of them, a tall man with a mustache, as we came past. He was holding his gray hat in his hands, looking at it as if he had never seen it before. "I'm terribly sorry. But do you know where I am? The last thing I remember, I was in a bakery in Manchester. Buying a cake. For my daughter's birthday." He looked around at the pink stone walls. "This isn't Manchester, is it?"
"No," said Uncle Tarık gently. "It's Turkey."
"Turkey!" The man looked astonished. "How on earth did I get to Turkey?"
Mordecai, leaning on Vex, looked at the man. His face did something very complicated.
"I'm sorry," he said, very quietly. "That was me. I'm so sorry."
The man looked at him, confused. "Do I know you?"

Mordecai shook his head. "No," he said. "But you will. I'll get you home. I promise. All of you." He looked around at the dozens of confused people in the tunnels, with their normal eyes. "I'll get every one of you home."

There were a lot of them. A lot of normal people, who had been Grays. A woman who taught piano in Oslo. A taxi driver from Lima. A student from Tokyo. A postman from Cairo, who had been missing for six years. A grandfather from Athens, who said his grandchildren would be very worried. They all came up with us, slowly, through the tunnels, up the stairs, floor after floor, a long, strange, confused procession, holding hands, helping each other.
Like a posada, I thought. In Mexico. Walking through the dark together. Looking for somewhere to stay.
Floor ten. Floor five. Floor two.
And then the top of the last staircase. And a door. And daylight.
We came out of Derinkuyu into the middle of the morning.

chapters.t: Chapter Thirty-One: The Sky Over Cappadocia
p: The sky was full of balloons.

Hundreds of them. More than I had ever seen. Every balloon in Cappadocia must have been in the sky. Red and yellow and blue and green and purple and striped and spotted, floating over the fairy chimneys, over the town, over the fields. The sun was shining on them, turning them into lanterns.
And above the balloons, higher, much higher, across the whole width of the sky, there were rainbows.
Seven of them.

Seven rainbows. One in each direction. Silver and purple and orange and blue and red-gold and green and gold. Stretching from one side of the world to the other. Crossing in the middle. Right above our heads. Making a shape.
A seven-pointed star.
A compass rose. Made of light. Filling the whole sky.

Everyone in the town of Derinkuyu was out in the street, looking up. Shopkeepers in their doorways. Old men outside the café. Children on their parents' shoulders. A man selling simit from a cart, with his mouth open. Everyone. Pointing. Taking photos. Crying. Laughing.
*Thank you, Windborn,* said every wind in the sky, all at once. Faint and far away and happy. *Thank you. Thank you.*
And then, from above, came a voice. Shouting. Through a megaphone.
"KUZEY AYDIN!"
We all looked up.
A big red balloon was floating very low over the town. Right above us. With an old man in the basket, with a huge white moustache, waving.
And dangling under the basket, on a rope, with a loop around his middle, swinging gently in the breeze, was a man in a gray suit. With brown eyes. Looking extremely confused. And quite happy.
"HE WOKE UP!" Hasan Amca shouted down, through the megaphone. "ABOUT AN HOUR AGO! HIS NAME IS DAVID! HE'S AN ACCOUNTANT FROM SCOTLAND! HE SAYS THIS IS THE BEST DAY OF HIS LIFE!"
"IT IS!" shouted David, from the end of the rope, waving both arms. "IT REALLY IS! THE VIEW IS INCREDIBLE!"
Bora sat down on the pavement and laughed until he cried.
And Grandma Nermin stood in the street of Derinkuyu, in the sunshine, with her face turned up to the sky. To the seven rainbows. To the balloons. To the winds.
She closed her eyes. She breathed in. A long, deep breath. The first breath of real air, of sky air, of free air, in two months.
Then she opened her eyes and looked at me.
"Well," she said. "That was exciting, wasn't it?"

chapters.t: Chapter Thirty-Two: The Day the Winds Came Home
p: *Kuzey didn't see any of this. But over the next few months, letters and postcards and phone calls and messages came, from all over the world. And Ela glued every one of them into the Clue Book. This is what they said.*

In the Basilica Cistern, in Istanbul, the ticket man who had once told the police there was an earthquake was sitting at his desk, half asleep, when a breeze came down the stairs. It swept through the stone forest, past three hundred and thirty-six columns, past the upside-down Medusa, and every single orange light turned on its stand, all by itself, *clank, clank, clank,* and pointed up at the ceiling, and made it glow like a sunrise. The goldfish all came to the surface at once. The ticket man said it was the most beautiful thing he had ever seen. He also said it was probably another earthquake.

In the Grand Bazaar, every carpet in the street of the carpet sellers lifted off its hook, and floated, and turned once in the air, very gently, and settled back down. Nobody was hurt. The carpet sellers said it was the best advertising they had ever had.

In Athens, at the Tower of the Winds, a tour guide was explaining the eight carved wind gods to a group of schoolchildren when all eight winds came down from the tower at once, laughing, and blew every child's hat off, and then put every hat back on, on the wrong child. The children screamed with joy. The tour guide had to sit down.

In the White Mountains of Crete, an old shepherd named Yiorgos looked out of his stone hut and saw a huge, shaggy creature with horns standing in the snow, with its face turned up to the sky, and its arms spread out wide. Laughing. A deep, rumbling laugh, like a cello. Around it, three hundred goats were dancing.

Under the palace of Knossos, in a cave that no one has visited since, a bronze giant sat against the wall with his knees pulled up and his eyes closed. And a warm wind came down the stairs, and wrapped around him, and the flowers on his fingers bloomed. Hundreds of them. Little yellow ones. The color of golden light. We know, because Asterion went back to see. He told a seal. The seal told a heron. The heron told a cat. The cat told Bora.

In Iceland, at the edge of the black beach at Vík, the three troll rocks stood in the waves as they had for a thousand years. And a wind came off the sea, and blew around them, three times. And a little boy called Siggi, standing on the beach with his grandfather, swore that he saw one of them wink.

Above Þingvellir, a very large raven flew in circles over the rift between the continents, screaming *KRAA! KRAA! KRAA!* at the top of his voice, for an hour. The other ravens said he was telling everyone that his best friend did it. He did it. He freed the winds. And that he, Krummi, the cleverest raven in Iceland, had helped. A lot. Mostly him, actually.

In Reykjavík, an old woman with white braids opened her front door and stood on her step and let the wind blow through her hair. And she said, out loud, to nobody, "Well done, Nermin's boy. Well done." And then she went inside and made soup.

In Egypt, on the Giza plateau, a scruffy brown camel called Mustafa stopped in the middle of carrying a tourist, and turned his head toward the north, and made a long, happy, gurgling sound like a drain unblocking. And then he sat down. On the tourist's foot. And refused to get up for an hour. His owner said he had never seen him look so pleased.

And the Sphinx, they say, the great stone lion with the head of a pharaoh, who has looked out at the sunrise for five thousand years, smiled. Just a little. Very slightly. If you look at it in the right light, at the right time, they say you can still see it.
In the Egyptian Museum, all the cats came out at once and sat on the steps in the sun. Dr. Amira counted sixty-three.

On the Nile, a little felucca with a white sail filled with wind on a day when there was no wind at all, and sailed all the way to the next village by itself, with an old man asleep in the bottom of it, snoring, with his turban over his face.

In Japan, at Fushimi Inari, ten thousand orange gates hummed like a choir. And a white fox with three tails sat on the top of a small, faded gate with a foreign name written on the back, and swished her tails, and looked very, very smug.

On Mount Kurama, the King of the Tengu stood on the highest cedar, with his huge black wings spread wide, and let the wind lift him, up and up, higher than he had flown in a thousand years. Below him, the young crow-tengu cawed and clacked their beaks. And Sōjōbō shouted something into the sky that sounded a lot like, "ABOUT TIME!"

On the top of Mount Fuji, Fūjin opened his great white bag, and turned it upside down, and shook it. And every wind inside it poured out, free, laughing. And for the first time in nine hundred years, he didn't have to hold them. He sat down in the snow next to his brother, and Raijin played the drums, softly, a happy rhythm. And they watched the winds go.

In Mexico, under the city of the gods, a great feathered serpent rose out of the dark pit, and up through the tunnel of stars, and out of the hole at the foot of its own temple, and into the sky. For the first time in fifteen hundred years. It flew over Teotihuacan, green and gold, with its feathers streaming, sweeping the road clear. And behind it, the rain came. Gentle. Warm. Exactly where it was needed.
In the canals of Xochimilco, the ice that had held a family of sleeping axolotls melted all at once. And they woke up. And swam. Smiling, the way axolotls always do.

And in a square in Coyoacán, by a fountain shaped like two coyotes, a very old man sitting under a tree full of kites felt the wind change. He looked up. Every kite in the tree was flying. All by themselves. Up off the branches, into the blue sky, dancing on their strings. Hundreds of them. Birds and suns and skulls with flowers.
Don Tomás took off his hat, and held it against his chest.
"The kites are still flying, Nermin," he said. "The kites are still flying."
It took a week to get everyone home.

All the people who had been Grays. There were three hundred and twelve of them, in the end. From forty-seven countries. Mordecai sat in a little hotel room in Göreme, every day, with a phone and a laptop and a long list of names, calling families. Embassies. Police stations. Hospitals. Arranging plane tickets. Paying for every single one, with his own money.
He didn't sleep much that week. He looked terrible. Gray and thin and tired.
But he never stopped. Not once. Not until the last one was home.

The last one was David, the accountant from Scotland. He didn't want to go home. He wanted to stay in Cappadocia and learn to fly balloons with Hasan Amca. In the end, he did. Hasan Amca says he's very good.
We went back to Istanbul on the bus. All of us. Grandma and me and Ela and Bora and Uncle Tarık. And Vera and Vex.
And Mordecai.
Nobody asked him to come. Nobody told him he couldn't. He just got on the bus, at the very end, and sat in the back seat, alone, with his hands in his lap, and looked out of the window for ten hours.

The *muavin* came round with tea and lemon cologne. Mordecai held out his hands for the cologne. Both hands. His two real hands. And when the muavin poured the cologne into them, he closed his eyes and breathed in the smell of lemons, as if it was the most wonderful thing he had ever smelled.

Grandma sat next to me. She held my hand the whole way. She slept a lot. When she woke up, she asked me questions. About everything. Every single thing. The cistern and the carpets and the Minotaur and the trolls and the Sphinx and the typhoon and the pit. She wanted to know it all.
When I told her about the typhoon, and the song, she cried.
When I told her about Fūjin, and the cards, she laughed so loudly that the whole bus turned around.
"He still thinks I cheated?" she said. "After forty years?"
"He wants a rematch," I said. "He told me to tell you."
"Of course he does," said Grandma. Then she leaned close to me, and whispered, "I did cheat, a little. Don't tell him."
When we got to Istanbul, Grandma walked into her flat in Kadıköy, and stood in the kitchen doorway, and looked around.

At the teacups. At her apron. At the crossword. At the nine compasses on the shelf, in the right order. At Paşa, who came running across the floor so fast that he slid on the tiles, and crashed into her legs, and then pretended he had meant to do it.
At the kettle on the stove. Boiling. Singing.
Mrs. Aksoy from downstairs had come up and lit it, as soon as she heard we were coming.
Grandma Nermin stood there for a long time.
Then she took off her coat, and hung it on the hook by the door. And she put on her apron. And she picked up Paşa. And she said, to nobody, to the whole kitchen, to the wind at the window:
"Right. Who wants börek?"
Three weeks later, on New Year's Day, the kettle in Grandma's kitchen in Kadıköy was whistling again.

It was a Sunday. The window was open, even though it was cold. The North Wind came in off the Bosphorus, smelling of salt and seagulls, and rattled the teacups on their saucers, the way it always did.

But it wasn't the same North Wind. Not exactly. It was freer, now. Lighter. It came in and went out and came in again, playing with the curtains, as if it was visiting because it wanted to. Not because anybody made it.
*Hello, Kuzey,* it said, when it came in. Just like that. Every morning. *Hello.*
*Hello,* I always said back.
The table was crowded.

My mom and dad were there. They had come home two days before, from the bottom of the world, with sunburned faces and suitcases full of penguin photos. My dad had brought a huge picture of the penguin. He said it was the same penguin. My mom said it wasn't. They argued about it all through lunch.
The night they came home, I gave them my letter. The one I wrote in Japan, on a page from the Clue Book, by the window, with Mount Fuji outside.
My mom read it first. Then my dad. Then my mom again. Then they both looked at me for a very long time. Then they looked at Grandma.
And Grandma said, "Well. I suppose you'd better sit down. It's a long story. Shall I make tea?"
We talked until four in the morning.

They believe me. Most of it. My dad still thinks the Minotaur was "probably a very large goat." Then I breathe on his tea, and it freezes, a little. I can still do that, a little bit. Just a little. The North Wind comes and visits, sometimes, and helps me, because it wants to. Not because it has to. My dad stares at his frozen tea every time and says, "Okay. Okay. Maybe not a goat."
Ela was there, at the table, with the Clue Book. It's full now. Every page. There's a new chapter at the very end, after THE ANSWER. It's called *WHAT HAPPENED NEXT.* She's still writing it.

Bora was there, on his fourth piece of börek. He has a new hat. A bigger one. With Krummi's feather and Shiro's hair, and a scale from the Feathered Serpent that he found on the floor of the chamber under the temple, and a camel hair from Mustafa that he says he kept in his pocket "for luck." He wears his golden wrestling mask on special occasions. This was a special occasion. He took it off to eat.

Uncle Tarık was there, explaining his paper to my dad, who wasn't listening, because he was arguing with my mom about the penguin. The paper is called *Evidence of a Byzantine Wind Chamber Beneath the Serpent Column, With Notes on Certain Unusual Events.* It is four hundred pages long. Nobody has believed a single word of it. He doesn't care. He says he knows it's true, and that's enough.
Dr. Amira was there, on a video call from Cairo, on Uncle Tarık's laptop, propped up against the teapot. She was holding up a museum cat. A little gray one. It had followed her home.

Rıza Usta was there. In person. He had climbed all five floors of stairs, at ninety years old, because he refused to use the elevator. "I don't trust it," he said. "It's never been in the Order." He brought Grandma a new compass. A beautiful one. With seven points.
Guðrún had sent a box from Iceland. Full of dried fish and skyr and a jar of something that smelled terrible. Bora said it was fermented shark. He opened it and closed it again very fast.

Fūjin had sent a postcard. From Mount Fuji. It had a picture of the mountain on the front, and on the back, in huge, messy, windy handwriting, it said: *REMATCH. CARDS. NEXT SUMMER. NO CHEATING THIS TIME, NERMIN. P.S. SŌJŌBŌ SAYS THE BOY STILL OWES HIM PRACTICE. A HUNDRED YEARS.*
Grandma laughed so hard when she read it that she had to sit down.
Vera and Vex were there. They come every Sunday now.

They live in Istanbul. In a flat near the sea, in Moda, near Uncle Tarık. With their father. Vera goes to my school now. She's in Ela's class. They sit together. They have seventeen secret codes. Nobody is allowed to know any of them.

Vera wants to be a marine biologist. My mom and dad are teaching her. They're taking her on their next research trip, in the summer. To the Black Sea. To count dolphins. She's so excited that she can't talk about anything else. Ela says it's very annoying. Ela is very happy.

Vex is quieter. He smiles more now, though. Small smiles. Not his father's smile. His own. He goes to Bora's house a lot. Bora's mother feeds him. Bora's mother says he is "still too thin." Bora's mother says that about everyone.
Vex has started flying kites. On the roof of their building, on Sunday afternoons. With his father.
And Mordecai Vane was there.
At the very end of the table. In an ordinary blue sweater. Holding a glass of tea with both of his ordinary hands. With two sugars.
Grandma had invited him. The first Sunday. "Forty years is a long time to be lonely," she said. "It's time he had tea with friends."
He doesn't talk much yet. He's still very thin. He still looks tired. Sometimes, at the table, he goes very quiet, and looks at his hands, for a long time, as if he can't believe they're his.
But every time the wind comes through the window, he closes his eyes.
And he smiles.

Around his neck, he wears a scarf. Blue, with little white flowers. A bit lumpy. A bit uneven. Grandma knitted it for him, the week after we came home. From the wool she unraveled in the underground city. She found the whole thread, still lying on the stairs, all the way down to the bottom. She brought it home in her pocket and knitted it again.
"For someone special," she said, when she gave it to him.
He hasn't taken it off since.
The weather has been strange since that day in Cappadocia.
Not bad. Just... friendlier.

Typhoons that turn away from cities at the very last second, and rain themselves out over the empty ocean. Rain that falls exactly where the farmers need it. A breeze that blows every time a kid is too hot on a playground. Kites that never, ever get stuck in trees. Fishermen on the Galata Bridge who say the fish have never been so good. A shepherd in Crete who says the snow on the White Mountains came early this year, "as if someone asked for it."
The scientists on TV can't explain it.
We can.
After lunch, Grandma and I stood at the window together, watching the ferries cross the Bosphorus. The seagulls were flying. The sun was going down, turning the water gold.
"Do you miss them?" she asked. "The Keys? The winds? The power?"
I thought about it.
Then I held up my hand. And a little breeze came in through the window, all by itself, and curled around my fingers. Like a cat. Warm. Gentle. It smelled of the sea.
I didn't call it. It just came. Because it wanted to.
"No," I said. "They're still here. They're just not mine anymore. They're everybody's."
Grandma laughed, and kissed the top of my head.

"That," she said, "is the only right answer. The only one. In nine hundred years, you're the first one who ever said it." She put her arm around my shoulders. "You'll make a very good Keeper one day, Kuzey Aydın."
"There's nothing left to keep," I said. "The Keys are gone."
"Oh, my love," said Grandma Nermin. "The Keys were never the important part."
She squeezed my shoulder.
"The important part," she said, "was always the asking."

And outside, the North Wind laughed with her. And blew across the Bosphorus, free, the way it had before there were Keys, the way it always would. Out over the ferries, and the bridges, and the domes, and the minarets. Out over the Black Sea, and the mountains, and the deserts, and the oceans.
Out over the whole wide world.
§END The End.

For hundreds of years, sailors on the Black Sea, the Bosphorus and the Mediterranean used a wind rose to name the winds. Each wind had its own name and its own personality, and every sailor knew them by heart. These are the seven winds of the Order of the Compass Rose.
**Yıldız (North).** Named after the North Star, *yıldız* means "star." A cold, clear, starry wind. Kuzey's own wind.
**Poyraz (Northeast).** The great wind of the Black Sea. When the Poyraz blows hard, the fishermen go home and the ferries rock.
**Gündoğusu (East).** "Sunrise." The wind that comes from where the sun is born each morning.
**Keşişleme (Southeast).** Named after the monks, the *keşiş,* who lived on the mountains to the southeast. A warm, dry wind from the deserts.
**Kıble (South).** The wind from the direction of Mecca. Hot, and full of sand.
**Lodos (Southwest).** A warm, wild, wet wind that brings big waves and headaches. People in Istanbul say the Lodos makes everyone grumpy.
**Karayel (Northwest).** "Black wind." A stormy, dark wind that brings clouds and sudden rain.
And the eighth, the west wind, the **Batı**, the one that would not make a deal? Nobody knows. It is still wild. That is another story.
Almost every place in *Kuzey and the Seven Winds* is real. You can visit them. (The giants, trolls, foxes and wind gods are harder to find. But you never know.)

**The Basilica Cistern, Istanbul.** A real underground water palace, about fifteen hundred years old, with 336 columns. Two of them really do stand on the heads of Medusa, one sideways and one upside down. Nobody is sure why.

**Galata Tower, Istanbul.** Built in 1348. Fire watchers really did live at the top. And there really is a story that a man named Hezarfen Ahmed Çelebi flew from it across the Bosphorus with wings he made himself.

**The Serpent Column, Istanbul.** A bronze column made of three twisted snakes, brought from Delphi in Greece, about 2,500 years old. The heads were broken off long ago. One is in the Istanbul Archaeology Museum.

**The Tower of the Winds, Athens.** A real eight-sided marble tower, about 2,000 years old, with a wind god carved on each side, and sundials underneath. Lips, the southwest wind, really is holding the back of a ship.
**Knossos, Crete.** The palace of the Minoans, nearly 4,000 years old, with its throne room, its painted dolphins and its red columns. The Minoans really did leap over bulls.
**Þingvellir, Iceland.** The rift valley where the North American and Eurasian plates are pulling apart, and where the Vikings held their parliament more than a thousand years ago.
**Strokkur, Iceland.** A real geyser. It really does erupt every few minutes.

**The Sphinx and the Pyramids, Giza, Egypt.** The Great Pyramid really was the tallest building on Earth for almost 4,000 years. The Sphinx really has lost its nose. Nobody has ever asked it for a second riddle. As far as we know.

**Fushimi Inari, Kyoto, Japan.** A shrine with thousands of orange torii gates winding up a mountain, and fox statues everywhere. The names of the people who donated the gates really are written on the back.
**Mount Kurama, Japan.** A real mountain north of Kyoto, with a real Path of Roots, and a real legend about the tengu king Sōjōbō teaching a boy to fight and fly.

**Teotihuacan, Mexico.** The city of the gods, with its Pyramid of the Sun, Pyramid of the Moon, Avenue of the Dead and Temple of the Feathered Serpent, covered in carved serpent heads. A real tunnel was found under the temple, with walls that glittered with pyrite and, at the bottom, real pools of liquid mercury.
**Xochimilco, Mexico City.** Canals and floating gardens from the time of the Aztecs, with brightly painted boats. Axolotls really do live there, and almost nowhere else in the world.

**Derinkuyu, Cappadocia, Turkey.** A real underground city, more than 80 meters deep, where thousands of people could hide, with real air shafts and real round stone doors. Nobody has ever found a Gate at the bottom.
But then, nobody has ever looked for one with a Windborn.
